sources.title: Nâzım Hikmet (Q184906), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'Nâzım Hikmet', description 'Turkish communist poet, playwright and novelist (1902-1963)', Korean label 나짐 히크메트, instance of human, born 15 January 1902 (an alternate value of 30 November 1901 is also recorded), died 3 June 1963, citizenship recorded as Ottoman Empire, Turkey and Poland. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.
Wikipedia, 'Nâzım Hikmet' (raw text opened for orientation on dates and the birth-date discrepancy). Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Gale biographical entry 'Hikmet, Nazim' reproduced on Encyclopedia.com (read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls him posthumously one of the giants of twentieth-century Turkish literature, whose poems, plays and prose were banned in Turkey for most of his life; says he revolutionized Turkish verse by challenging traditional forms with broken lines and a street-vernacular style, and was the first Turkish poet to win an international reputation; sentenced in 1938 and held until 1950, with sources contradicting each other on the charge and on how his prison time ended; writes that his most ambitious project, the five-volume Human Landscapes of nearly twenty thousand lines, was written in prison between 1938 and 1950 and published only after his death; quotes critics (Halman, Andrews, Konuk) and his own remark that the artist is 'the engineer of the human soul'. Reference entry that leans on critics' judgments; admiring, and openly notes contradictory accounts.

EBSCO Research Starters, 'Nazim Hikmet' (a Salem Press literary biography; read in full): imprisonment of seventeen years in total; the 1938 arraignment for inciting unrest in the armed forces after cadets were found with his poems; the epic Human Landscapes begun in Bursa prison and circulated in parts among friends and family, with some portions confiscated; a 1949 hunger strike of seventeen days after a heart attack; release in 1950, then a conscription order, and flight alone in a small fishing boat to a Romanian ship in 1951; work as proofreader, translator and scriptwriter and publication of columns under a pseudonym; plays that experimented with old and new forms and that drew criticism for facile identification of characters with political positions; a play of the 1950s that took issue with the personality cult and rigid criticism of the Stalin era, yet the author is also said to have continued to uphold Soviet positions on international security, with some late works doing him little credit. Scholarly reference biography with critical remarks.

Poetry Foundation, 'Nazim Hikmet' biography page (read): left Turkey after the First World War to study in Moscow, became a Marxist; arrested after returning in 1924, escaped to Russia, came back in 1928; in the next ten years wrote many works including the 1936 Epic of Shaykh Bedreddin and the 20,000-line Human Landscapes; shifted from syllabic patriotic verse to plainer language and Turkish folk traditions; left in 1951 after long imprisonment; his works were banned in Turkey until 1965. Short institutional biography.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Nazim Hikmet' (read): calls him one of the most important and influential figures in twentieth-century Turkish literature; briefly attended the naval academy, studied in Moscow, returned a Marxist in 1924; his mastery of language and introduction of free verse and a wide range of themes influenced Turkish literature in the late 1930s; influenced by the Russian Futurists he tried to 'depoetize' poetry, later with a quieter style; the Epic of Shaykh Bedreddin (1936) and the 20,000-line Portraits of People from My Land; also plays in vigorous prose. Short reference article.

Hurriyet Daily News, 'Poems of freedom from behind iron bars, exile' (7 January 2009, on the restoration of his citizenship; read in full): chronology of the 1925 conviction after which he fled, a 1928 return and detention, his 1931 trial in which he is quoted answering that he was a communist poet and was found not guilty, the 1933 conviction, the 1938 arrest and sentences combined to 28 years and 4 months, the newspaper campaign of 1949, several hunger strikes and hospitalizations, release in 1950 after 12 years and 7 months, and the report that poems written in prison were smuggled abroad. Turkish newspaper summary.

Daily Sabah (Hakan Arslanbenzer), 'Nazim Hikmet: Human scenes from my homeland' (17 October 2015; read in full): early life, the 1925 court sentence and flight, a 1928 attempt to cross the border illegally that ended in several months of detention, the 1938 life sentence in the Navy Case, flight to Romania in 1951 and loss of citizenship; argues his poetry worked as a propaganda tool for the Turkish left for decades, yet says critics of every political view accept him as a major poet for his fluent, natural Turkish, and that Human Landscapes draws its power from portraits of Anatolian villagers he met in prison. Opinion feature that is openly critical of the poet's use of verse as propaganda while praising his language.

Republic of Turkiye Ministry of Culture and Tourism, biography pages 'Nazim Hikmet' (two pages read): navy school and discharge for ill health, the 1921 move to Anatolia and then Moscow, the 1925 verdict in absentia and flight, the 1928 detention at Hopa, newspaper and film-studio work and the use of the pen name Orhan Selim, the 1938 sentences reduced to 28 years and four months, a hunger strike that came with a campaign for amnesty, release in 1950 'after 13 years of imprisonment' (the second page says about 12 years), flight in 1951 on a Romanian vessel via a motorboat, publication of poems under pseudonyms in the 1940s, list of works across poetry, plays, novels, letters and fairy tales, and the 2002 'Year of Nazim'. State-run biography page; its figures differ slightly from other sources.

persistence.rationale: [src_hikmet_gale, src_hikmet_salem, src_hikmet_hurriyet, src_hikmet_ktb | 1938-1950 | reference entry, scholarly biography, newspaper summary, state biography] Four accounts agree that he spent roughly twelve to thirteen years in prison from 1938 and that the long epic of nearly twenty thousand lines was written during those years, some parts circulating in manuscript among friends and some confiscated. Sources contradict each other on charges and release details, and the accounts retell one prison narrative, so the score stays in the low 70s with moderate confidence.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_hikmet_gale, src_hikmet_britannica, src_hikmet_salem, src_hikmet_sabah | 1920s-1940s | reference entries, scholarly biography, newspaper feature] Reference entries credit him with introducing free verse with broken lines, a colloquial register and contemporary subject matter into Turkish poetry, and the Salem biography adds distinctive combinations of folk song, saga and Soviet models. The judgment of originality rests on critics' assessment of his place in literary history rather than on independent behavioral episodes, so confidence is capped.

experimentation.rationale: [src_hikmet_britannica, src_hikmet_salem, src_hikmet_gale | 1920s-1945 | reference article, scholarly biography, reference entry] Three accounts describe his deliberate departure from syllabic meter under Futurist influence, his attempt to 'depoetize' poetry, his later turn to quatrains in the 1945 Rubaiyat poems to argue with the Persian model, and plays that tried old and new technical forms. These are a stylistic record described by critics, not a documented series of trials and revisions.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_hikmet_gale, src_hikmet_salem, src_hikmet_sabah | 1930s-1950s | reference entry, scholarly biography, newspaper feature] Critics describe musical qualities and strong visual imagery in his verse, use of vowel harmony and folk song, and a fluent daily-speech Turkish. These are critics' characterizations of his poems, not specific accounts of how he chose among forms, so the row is a modest inference.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_hikmet_salem, src_hikmet_gale, src_hikmet_britannica | 1920s-1950s | scholarly biography, reference entries] He rejected inherited Ottoman verse forms for a style of his own, and in exile wrote a play that took issue with the Stalin-era personality cult, although the same biography says he continued to uphold Soviet positions on international security and calls him not a literary conformist. The record is mixed and the independence is more clearly literary than political.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_hikmet_salem, src_hikmet_ktb, src_hikmet_hurriyet | 1928-1960 | scholarly biography, state biography, newspaper summary] He wrote poetry, plays, novels, essays and letters and earned a living as a journalist, film scriptwriter, translator and proofreader. All of it lies within writing, so this is range across literary forms rather than across unrelated fields.

adaptability.rationale: [src_hikmet_salem, src_hikmet_ktb, src_hikmet_hurriyet | 1930s-1950s | scholarly biography, state biography, newspaper summary] When his publishing was restricted he took work as proofreader, translator and scriptwriter, wrote columns under a pseudonym, turned to historical subjects such as the 1936 epic when contemporary topics were closed to him, and published poems under other names in the 1940s. Three accounts describe these shifts independently, though none quantifies them.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_hikmet_hurriyet, src_hikmet_salem, src_hikmet_ktb | 1938-1951 | newspaper summary, scholarly biography, state biography] Reports say prison poems were smuggled abroad, that the long epic circulated in parts among relatives and friends, that he published under pseudonyms, and that he left in 1951 by boat with the help of friends. The smuggling claim rests on one newspaper summary and the escape details differ between sources, and others supplied much of the means.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_hikmet_hurriyet, src_hikmet_sabah, src_hikmet_salem, src_hikmet_ktb | 1924-1951 | newspaper summary, newspaper feature, scholarly biography, state biography] Four accounts describe repeated returns to Turkey and publication after convictions, a 1928 attempt to cross the border illegally that ended in detention, hunger strikes during imprisonment (seventeen days in 1949 after a heart attack, per the Salem biography) and the 1951 flight in a small boat. The behavior is documented in several sources, but the details vary and it was driven by overlapping political circumstances.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_hikmet_hurriyet, src_hikmet_salem, src_hikmet_ktb | 1931-1950 | newspaper summary, scholarly biography, state biography] He faced repeated trials and convictions without recanting, is quoted in a 1931 trial affirming that he was a communist poet, went on hunger strike while imprisoned, and in exile wrote against Stalin-era dogmatism. The trial quotation comes from one newspaper summary, and the sources disagree on charges and outcomes.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_hikmet_gale, src_hikmet_salem | 1930s-1950s | reference entry, scholarly biography] The reference entry quotes his own statement that art is an active institution in society and the artist the engineer of the human soul, and critics read his commitments as growing from love of people; the Salem biography describes poems pressing social concerns across forms. Mostly his own statement and critics' reading, so the row is an inference.

provenance.notes: Roster70. portrait_preflight stageB PLAUSIBLE; LEAD SURVIVED: Deutsche Fotothek photograph by Hans-Joachim Koch, January 1956, shown through Commons and the Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek. Item-level CC BY-SA 4.0 was read in the DDB record during Stage B; on re-check both the DDB record and the Fotothek item page were behind a proof-of-work wall and were not bypassed. The Fotothek fee and usage terms were read from an Internet Archive snapshot (December 2024): usage of visual media is fee-based and subject to approval except for reduced-quality digital objects offered under a Creative Commons license (the page names CC BY-SA 3.0, whereas this item is recorded as 4.0), with a courtesy request to send the URL of online uses to the Fotothek. CAVEATS for lead review: license version 3.0 on the terms page vs 4.0 on the item record; the Commons structured date (14 September 1956) conflicts with the description and DDB (January 1956); shipping under CC BY-SA means the attribution line must stay with the image. SITTER: DDB title (read in Stage B) names Hikmet at the January 1956 Berlin congress with a GND-linked depicted person; Commons description and category agree; the image shows a man consistent with other known photographs of him, but no caption appears on the image itself. KIND likeness (photograph from a lifetime sitting). HISTORICAL ATTRIBUTION: attributable (extensive publications, trials and court records; many accounts agree on the main facts); sources disagree on birth date (official 15 January 1902, an alternate 1901 date), on charges and sentence lengths in the 1938 case, on how he left prison and on whether his prison time was 12 or 13 years. POLITICS: primary identity is poet and playwright; his party membership, trials and propaganda charges are context only and are not used to infer any trait beyond documented behavior (repeated trials, hunger strikes, flight); no row scores political belief, and later Soviet-bloc activity is not scored. Sources actually read: Encyclopedia.com Gale entry, EBSCO Research Starters (Salem), Poetry Foundation, Britannica, Hurriyet Daily News, Daily Sabah, Ministry of Culture and Tourism pages; Wikipedia raw text for orientation only. Not opened: Blasing's 2013 biography, Goksu and Timms 'Romantic Communist', Hikmet's own letters and poems. LIMITS: 11 rows; no source gives specific, independent episodes for planning, discipline or collaboration, so those are unscored.
